questions.q: Why can a technically correct security control still get rolled back under pressure?
options: Technically correct controls are never actually deployed
Business teams have no influence over whether a control stays enabled
Rollback pressure only happens when a control is incorrectly written
It can break a legitimate business workflow nobody mapped first, creating pressure strong enough to force a reversal
questions.explain: The warehouse scanner-to-email example shows a correctly built policy still colliding with a real workflow, which creates real pressure to revert it.

questions.q: What is a documented exception path, as described in this lesson?
options: A specific group, process, and approver for a logged, time-limited exclusion for a legitimate workflow
A method for bypassing peer review on future control changes
A feature that only exists for Conditional Access, not for any other control type
A way to permanently disable a security control for the entire organization
questions.explain: The exception path lets one affected team get a logged, time-boxed exclusion without the policy itself ever being disabled.

questions.q: Why does communicating a rollout before it happens reduce risk?
options: A help desk that expects the change can calmly handle the first failure instead of escalating it as an outage
Communication prevents the control from ever needing an exception path
It replaces the need for audit mode or report-only testing from Lesson 26
It has no real effect on how a rollout is received
questions.explain: An unexpected failure gets escalated as an outage, and outages are exactly what gets controls reverted quickly.

questions.q: What does a phased, wave-based rollout accomplish that jumping straight from pilot to everyone does not?
options: It guarantees the control will never need an exception
It skips the need for the pilot group from Lesson 26 entirely
Each wave carries a smaller blast radius and gives the exception process time to work before the next group hits the same issue
It makes the rollout happen faster than enforcing on everyone at once
questions.explain: Waves expand enforcement in stages, catching issues the first pilot missed before the remainder of the organization is affected.

questions.q: Why does a documented exception path protect a control better than simply disabling it for the one team with a problem?
options: There is no real difference between the two approaches
Disabling a policy for one team has no effect on anyone else
An exception path is slower and less effective than a full rollback
Disabling the whole policy undermines protection for everyone, while a logged exception fixes the one workflow without weakening the control elsewhere
questions.explain: The exception path keeps the control intact for the rest of the organization while resolving the specific legitimate workflow it broke.
